newsitem.title: CANADA: Tenke says work continues amid rebel push.
newsitem.headline: Tenke says work continues amid rebel push.

text.p: Zairean rebels swept past the rich Tenke Fungurume copper-cobalt property on Tuesday, but work continued normally at the site, Tenke Mining Corp President Ted Webb said.

"Everything is very peaceful," he said in a telephone interview from Tenke's London offices. "We haven't had any lost days or anything. We continue to map and survey the drill hole locations for the exploration program and build roads...it's business as usual."

Despite a rebel advance aimed at overthrowing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, Tenke is pressing ahead with plans to develop a US$1.3 billion copper and cobalt mine at the site in mineral-rich southeastern Shaba province.
Tenke signed a deal in December with Zaire's government to exploit the mammoth deposit, the first significant investment in the country by a private mining concern since the 1970s.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has sought to reassure Tenke and foreign companies, and executives said he had signalled that foreign investors would be welcome in the country.

Kabila's forces launched an effort to topple Mobutu six months ago and have captured control of a large swath of eastern Zaire. Their next main target is the city of Lubumbashi, capital of Shaba province southeast of the Tenke Fungurume property.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) fighters were headed east on Tuesday toward the town of Likasi after they left Tenke Fungurume, Webb said.
Asked if that meant the area around Tenke Fungurume was now under rebel control, Webb said: "I don't know whether I should answer that today. Let's say that the rebels have been through."

He said there were no clashes in the area. The rebels "were well received by the village of Fungurume, a lot of celebration. They were fed by the local people and they moved on to Likasi. Of course there's no sign of Zairean soldiers around any more. They have gone," Webb said.
The company plans to bring a group of 32 international mining analysts to the property on April 17 and then bring in two drill more drill rigs soon afterward.
Whether the analysts' trip went ahead depended on what happened in Lubumbashi over the next 36 hours, Webb said. The analysts would transfer to small planes at Lubumbashi to fly to Tenke Fungurume.
"We're clearly not going to fly them in there while there's a confrontation going on between the AFDL and the presidential guard," he said.
But "if Lubumbashi is in the hands of the AFDL, we certainly have no problems taking them."
